name: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Cyclic Compounds
what: This subtopic covers the structural features, homologous series and systematic IUPAC naming of alkanes (including branched isomers), alkenes, cyclohexane and benzene. It also introduces the concept of a homologous series and saturated versus unsaturated molecules.
why: Hydrocarbons form the backbone of all organic molecules. Mastering their naming rules provides the foundation for naming every other functional group family, since all organic compound names are built on the parent hydrocarbon chain.

items.title: I can describe the features of a homologous series and give examples
items.what: A homologous series is a sequence of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, where each member differs from the next by one –CH2– unit. All members share the same general formula.
items.why: Understanding homologous series lets you predict the properties of unfamiliar molecules by comparing them to known members of the same family, without needing to study each compound individually.
items.example: The alkane series (methane, ethane, propane, butane…) all have only C–C single bonds and follow the general formula CnH2n+2, with each member having one more CH2 than the previous.

items.title: I can name straight-chain and branched alkanes using IUPAC rules up to C8
items.what: Alkane names are based on the longest continuous carbon chain (parent hydrocarbon), ending in '-ane'. Alkyl branches are named as prefixes with their position number, and the chain is numbered from the end that gives the lowest locants to substituents.
items.why: Systematic naming ensures that every molecule has exactly one correct name and that any trained chemist can draw the structure from the name alone, enabling unambiguous communication.
items.example: The alkane with a 6-carbon chain and a methyl group on the third carbon is named 3-methylhexane, not 4-methylhexane, because the end closest to the branch is used for numbering.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alkanes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from a name, identify the parent chain length, draw the carbon skeleton, add any alkyl branches at their stated positions, and fill in all hydrogen atoms to satisfy four bonds per carbon.
items.why: Drawing structures from names is the reverse of naming and is equally tested in exams; it confirms that you understand what each part of a name represents structurally.
items.example: 2,4-dimethylhexane has a 6-carbon parent chain with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4. The skeletal formula is a 6-carbon zigzag with single-carbon branches at the second and fourth vertices.

items.title: I can name straight-chain and branched alkenes using IUPAC rules, specifying the position of the double bond
items.what: Alkene names end in '-ene' and include a number indicating the first carbon of the C=C double bond. The chain is numbered from the end closest to the double bond to give it the lowest possible locant.
items.why: Because positional isomers of alkenes are possible for chains of four or more carbons, specifying the double bond position is essential to identify the correct compound.
items.example: CH2=CHCH2CH3 is named but-1-ene, not but-3-ene, because the double bond begins at carbon 1 when the chain is numbered from the end closest to it.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alkenes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Drawing an alkene from its name requires placing the C=C double bond at the specified carbon position and ensuring the double bond carbon atoms each have the correct number of remaining bonds to hydrogen or other groups.
items.why: Drawing alkenes accurately, including the correct position and geometry of the double bond, is required for answering naming and structure questions in assessments.
items.example: 2-methylpent-2-ene has a 5-carbon chain with a double bond starting at carbon 2 and a methyl branch also at carbon 2. The skeletal formula shows a double bond between the second and third vertices with a branch at the second vertex.

items.title: I can describe the structure of cyclohexane and represent it using a skeletal formula
items.what: Cyclohexane (C6H12) is a saturated cyclic alkane in which six carbon atoms are connected in a ring, each bonded to two hydrogen atoms. Its skeletal formula is drawn as a regular hexagon with no double bonds.
items.why: Cyclohexane is a commonly encountered ring structure in chemistry and biochemistry, and understanding cyclic structures extends the naming and structural rules learned for straight-chain alkanes.
items.example: The skeletal formula of cyclohexane is a plain hexagon. Each vertex represents a CH2 group, and the molecular formula C6H12 confirms it is saturated despite not fitting the CnH2n+2 formula of open-chain alkanes.

items.title: I can describe the structure of benzene and explain why it is represented with a circle inside a hexagon
items.what: Benzene (C6H6) is a planar cyclic molecule in which each carbon contributes one electron to a ring of delocalised electrons above and below the plane. This is represented as a hexagon with a circle inside, or alternatively with three alternating double bonds.
items.why: The delocalised electron ring gives benzene greater stability than a typical alkene. Recognising benzene's unique structure is necessary for understanding its physical properties and later reaction chemistry.
items.example: Because benzene has a ring of delocalised electrons rather than fixed double bonds, it does not readily undergo addition reactions the way alkenes do, making it more chemically stable.
